Store the boundary as a number (the index size) at the very start: a fixed-size header. The general idea is a (custom) file format: compartments plus a header that says where each lies.
Magic name 8 B (OUR_DICT), version 4 B, index size 4 B; total 16 bytes.
Magic name lets a decoder tell at once it is our dictionary, not some other file. Version: one format can have variants (v1 index first, v2 data first); decoder reads it and acts accordingly.

Read first 16 bytes (header); first 8 say OUR_DICT; next 4 give version; next 4 give index size (3,502,000); read exactly that many bytes; build in-memory hash map; everything after is data the offsets point into; ready.
MP4 works the same way: the file records where its video and audio lie (compartments plus a directory/header); like PNG's 8 magic bytes.

NOT ON PAGE as a promise; page's preview: a key-value store on cheap disks that many use without knowing, name revealed at end.
Key-value store with put/get/delete written all day; each put persisted on disk before ack (no in-memory batching); as fast as the disk allows; on cheap magnetic hard disks.
SSD sits closer to memory in speed and cost; HDD slower and cheaper; bulk data on magnetic HDDs because SSDs cost too much.
Byte offset maps to a sector on a spinning platter; platter rotates and head moves to it. Mechanical movement (head seek + rotation) is slowest.
No collecting writes in memory and flushing in batches: a put must be on disk when acknowledged.
Append each put to the end of one file (fsync before ack); head is already at end, no seek: the bare minimum mechanical movement.
K1 V1' is appended at the end; old K1 V1 entry stays on disk, obsolete.
The file is append-only: writes only at the end; going back to the old value means a seek/in-place write which the design forbids.
DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1), a tombstone marker appended at the end; costs exactly a put, O(1).
Naive: scan all entries, return the latest for the key. Fast: in-memory hash table key -> offset of latest entry.
Reads anywhere (random reads), writes only at the end (no in-place writes).
K1->O1, K2->O2, K3->O3; PUT K1 V1' at O4 -> K1->O4; DEL K2 appends K2 -1 at O5 and removes K2 from map. Final: K1->O4, K3->O3.

Machine crashes while writing a big value, leaving a torn record; reader trusts value size, reads into the next record and returns garbage with no error.

Cyclic redundancy check: checksum over rest of record (timestamp, sizes, key, value), stored with it, recomputed on read. Put first so reader checks before trusting any byte. Bitcask and LevelDB log put it first; Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog use CRCs at other positions.
CRC | TS | KSZ | VSZ | K | V. TS is metadata for settling conflicts between versions of a key.
Ignore the entry (in merge/compaction and everywhere) as if never written; never append after a torn record; after crash write to a new file; rebuild stops reading the file at a failed CRC.
File id, entry/value size, offset (value position), timestamp. GET: hash table lookup, disk seek, disk read.
Bitcask's files are in write order, not sorted, so no two-pointer merge; use a temporary hash table (latest entry wins, deletes removed).
Limitation: every key must fit in memory. Strengths: O(1) put/get/delete, bare-minimum disk I/O, writes as fast as disk persists (I/O saturation), one seek per get, easy backups.
